item.title: Confessions of a Type A Girl (Part 1)
item.dc:creator: Margaret Cole
item.description: Part 1: what happens when your plan only works on a perfect day.
item.content:encoded:
As you can probably tell by now, I’d classify myself as fairly Type A. Just to make sure we’re all on the same page about what that means, here’s the textbook version:

As someone who runs marathons, wakes up at 5 a.m. every day, has lists for everything and is chronically on time, I’d say this is a pretty accurate classification. I’ve always prided myself on being Type A. Who wouldn’t want to get things done, be reliable and always be the most productive version of themselves? But as much as I love casually dropping into conversation everything I managed to accomplish in a given day, my life can often feel like one massive wave: incredible highs when I actually manage to get it all done, and intense lows when the most trivial things trigger my stress.

Perhaps some context would help?

A few weeks ago, I posted How I’m Starting My Winter Arc, where I laid out all the ways I wanted to elevate my life by the end of the year and the step-by-step approach I’d take to get there. In short, if I was actually going to accomplish it all, this is what an ordinary day would have to look like:

  • 5:00 a.m.: wake up
  • 5:00–5:15 a.m.: drink water and put on workout clothes
  • 5:15–6:15 a.m.: work out (running, cycling or weight lifting)
  • 6:15–6:45 a.m.: stretch, shower and get ready for work
  • 6:45–7:00 a.m.: make breakfast and coffee
  • 7:00–8:00 a.m.: one hour of focused work on VIRI
  • 8:00–8:15 a.m.: wrap up, pack lunch and head out the door
  • 8:15–8:45 a.m.: walk to work and call a friend or family member
  • 8:45 a.m.–5:00 p.m.: work (and drink 50 oz of water)
  • 5:00–5:30 p.m.: walk home
  • 5:30–6:15 p.m.: make and eat dinner (if I’m not eating meal prep)
  • 6:15–7:15 p.m.: one hour of focused coursework (an online business foundations certificate)
  • 7:15–7:45 p.m.: read
  • 7:45–8:15 p.m.: wind down and get ready for bed
  • 8:30 p.m.: asleep

As you can see, there’s quite a lot going on here. And this is a typical day.

Something to know about me: once I decide something is a priority, there’s no going back. So perhaps I was a bit ambitious when I decided what my winter arc would require, but being the overachiever that I am, it became my mission to prove I could do it all: work out, make consistent progress on VIRI, complete an online certificate and read. Every day. On top of my 9-to-5.

And the first few days went great! I actually managed to end each day with every item checked off the list. I woke up at 5, worked out, cranked out VIRI articles, worked my 9-to-5, cooked myself dinner, did over an hour of marketing coursework and read. I really was accomplishing everything I had put my mind to. Except… there was no breathing room. None. At all. Any wrench in the plan meant something had to give that day. And guess what? There are a surprising number of wrenches.

Travel, meetings, events, you name it. Within four days of starting my winter arc, they had all shown up, and they kept showing up almost every day, right up until today as I write this. So I had my four perfect days, and after that I became a duck: head calmly above the water, feet paddling for dear life underneath.

Take Sunday the 8th. I had an evening flight back to D.C. and wasn’t supposed to get home until around 9:30 p.m. That’s already about an hour after I usually go to bed, which meant that, even if nothing went wrong, I’d start the next day slightly sleep-deprived. But one hour isn’t too bad, right?

On the way to the airport, just for good measure, I refreshed the Delta app, and my cortisol immediately spiked. A yellow “delayed” warning told me my flight now wouldn’t land until 11 p.m. If I was lucky, I’d be in bed by midnight. I couldn’t even remember the last time I’d gone to bed at midnight.

My mind started to spiral.

Five hours of sleep? This is a complete disaster. I definitely can’t run tomorrow morning. I guess I can maybe write one article for VIRI before work. Oh my gosh, I’m going to be totally exhausted at work. I’m so not going to want to do my coursework and read after work either. Wait, do I have something after work tomorrow? Let me check. You’ve got to be kidding me, it’s our annual team dinner and it doesn’t end until 8! And I still have to meal prep! When am I going to have time for any of this? Well, I guess I can meal prep tomorrow morning before work. There go all of my priorities.

So yes, my flight was only delayed an hour and a half, but to my Type A brain, this was a national emergency.

That Sunday is perhaps an extreme example, but it shows how unpredictable life can blow holes in even the most ambitious plans. It became obvious that my plan for success only worked on a perfect day. And perfect days happen very, very rarely, if at all.

My ambitions haven’t gone anywhere, but my definition of success clearly needs some adjusting. As much as I’d love to check every one of my aspirations off a daily to-do list, most of the time that’s an unrealistic expectation, and meeting it takes a rigidity that leaves no room for real life. So going forward, here’s what I’m doing differently:

1. Giving each day a range

Instead of expecting myself to hit every priority every day, I need success to look much more holistic. On days when meetings or life events come up, success can mean finishing two of my four extra priorities instead of all of them. If I somehow find the time to do all four, amazing, but that shouldn’t be the expectation every day.

2. Setting weekly goals instead of daily ones

Daily time goals were a big part of the stress I was starting to feel, especially because whenever I missed one day’s goal, it felt like it had to be piled onto the next. Bigger weekly goals give me the flexibility to get things done in a more realistic way, one that accounts for day-to-day disruptions.

For instance, rather than making “work on VIRI for one hour” my daily goal, I can set a weekly goal to “write three VIRI articles” or “complete five hours of focused VIRI work.”

Here’s what that looks like side by side:

Revising my expectations wasn’t fun, and admitting that the plan I was so proud of only worked on a perfect day was even less fun. Humility has never been one of my greatest strengths. But I’ve realized that being Type A was never really the problem. A plan with no breathing room was.

So I’m still a proud Type A girly, just with “flexibility” newly added to my vocabulary. I’ll be living by the revised schedule for the next few weeks, and in Part 2, I’ll report back on whether a Type A girl can actually learn to go with the flow (or at least paddle a little less).

Until then, if you’re a fellow list-making, 5 a.m.-alarm-setting, chronically on-time overachiever, ask yourself: what’s one thing you could give a range instead of a rule this week? And if you want to build your own winter arc with the breathing room included from the start, the free planner takes about a minute.
